paragraphs: Many bacteria regulate certain genes according to the abundance of their own kind. Each cell releases a small signaling molecule, and only when the molecule's concentration crosses a threshold do the cells switch on behaviors, such as secreting digestive enzymes or emitting light, that would be futile if a lone cell attempted them. The standard account of this quorum sensing treats the signal as a census: the molecule mediates between the size of the population and the decision to act. Because the products the system governs are public goods, benefiting every cell nearby whether or not it helped to make them, quorum sensing has also become a favorite puzzle for students of microbial altruism. A mutant that enjoys the enzyme but declines to produce it ought to prosper at the expense of its neighbors and, in time, to nullify the arrangement on which it depends.

Yet the census reading assumes that the concentration of the signal tracks the number of cells, and often it does not. In a confined pore of soil a handful of cells can reach the threshold, because the molecule cannot diffuse away; in an open current a dense population may never reach it. Some microbiologists therefore propose that what the signal measures is not density but diffusion, that is, whether secreted products will stay close enough to repay their cost. On this view the cheater problem is less acute than it appears, for the conditions that trigger production are those of close propinquity, in which a cell's products return disproportionately to itself and its clonal kin. The two readings need not be rivals. A cell cannot tell crowding from confinement, and it has no need to, since either condition signals that secretion is likely to pay.

When the polymath Francis Galton compared the heights of parents with those of their grown children in the 1880s, he found that unusually tall parents tended to have children who were tall but less so, and that unusually short parents tended to have children who were short but less so. Galton called the pattern “regression toward mediocrity” and took it to reveal a hereditary force that drew each lineage back toward the type of its ancestors. Later statisticians showed that no such force is needed: whenever two measurements are imperfectly correlated, extreme values of one will on average be paired with less extreme values of the other, simply because an extreme value owes part of its extremity to influences that the two measurements do not share. Nor could Galton's force account for a fact his own tables contained: the pattern runs backward as well as forward, so that unusually tall children have parents who are, on average, less tall than they are. Galton's misreading proved paradigmatic, and it recurs wherever a group is chosen because of an extreme score: the schools with the worst results improve the next year, the patients who enroll in a trial when their symptoms peak report relief, and neither change by itself portends anything about the remedy applied. To interrogate a claim of improvement, then, one must first ask how the group came to be chosen.

For economists from Adam Smith onward, the craft guilds of early modern Europe were cartels in ceremonial dress: associations of masters that limited entry to their trades, fixed prices and lambasted any outsider who undersold them, all on the pretext of protecting the public from shoddy work. A generation of revisionist historians has replied that the pretext was often real. Where a buyer could not judge a bolt of cloth or a silver cup before paying for it, the guild's mark and its inspections supplied information that the market could not, and the long apprenticeship the guild required transmitted skills that no written manual could convey.

Both accounts, however, treat the guild as a single actor whose interests can be set against those of its customers, and the records of the guild courts tell a more factious story. In city after city the bulk of the litigation pitted masters not against interlopers but against their own journeymen: over wages, over the length of the working day and, above all, over the terms of admission to mastership. As the cost of the masterpiece, the entry fee and the obligatory banquet rose through the seventeenth century, the very standards that the revisionists credit with protecting buyers also kept the number of masters small, and the sons and sons-in-law of masters were routinely excused from them. Journeymen answered with brotherhoods of their own, which boycotted workshops that had earned their ire, ousted strikebreakers from the lodging houses and could close a town's trade for weeks.

None of this shows that the revisionists are wrong about information or training; a rule can protect buyers and exclude rivals at once. What it shows is that the question of whom the guild served has no single answer, because the guild was less an actor than an arena, a structure within which masters and journeymen contended, often in internecine fashion, over the pecuniary value of skill. To read a guild's statutes either as the charter of a cartel or as the curriculum of a school is to mistake the record of a settlement, frequently a temporary one, for the intention of a single party.

Western collectors who began buying Japanese woodblock prints in the 1860s brought with them a habit of mind formed by European painting: a picture was the work of the person who conceived it, and the name worth knowing was the one on the sheet. Under that habit the landscapes of Hiroshige, whom many of them ranked as nonpareil, and the actor portraits of Sharaku were catalogued as theirs alone, although the designer's part in a print was a brush drawing on thin paper that was pasted face down on a block of cherry wood and destroyed when the carver cut through it. The carver decided how the drawn line would be limned in wood, whether a stroke the brush had inflected, swelling and tapering, would keep that modulation or stiffen into an even contour; and the printer, working from a few spoken instructions and a proof or two, decided how a gradation of blue would fade across a sky. The publisher, who commissioned the design, paid for the blocks and judged when they were too worn to print from, is seldom mentioned at all.

It would be easy to conclude that the designer's preeminence is a fiction imposed by foreign buyers, and some recent scholarship, irreverent toward the old catalogues, comes close to saying so. But it was the publishers who put the designer's signature on the sheet and who advertised new series under the names of designers popular enough to sell them; carvers and printers, though now and then identified by a small seal, were never advertised. The cult of the designer, in other words, was not simply imported. What the collectors added was the assumption that the name on a print identifies the source of every quality a viewer admires in it, so that a sky whose gradation is prized in one impression and missing from a later one was taken as evidence of the designer's genius or decline rather than of a printer's skill or a publisher's decision to economize.

When a population of bacteria is exposed to a lethal dose of an antibiotic, most cells die quickly, but the killing then slows: a small fraction survives for hours or days and, once the drug is withdrawn, regrows into a population as susceptible as the original. These survivors, called persisters, are not resistant mutants, since their offspring inherit no protection. For decades persisters were explained as dormant cells that escape drugs acting only on growing cells simply because they are not growing. The explanation had a palpable clinical appeal, for it implied that waking persisters before treatment would leave them vulnerable.

Yet when microbiologists tracked single cells under the microscope, they found that many persisters had been dividing just before the drug arrived and that many dormant cells died. Dormancy, it now appears, is neither necessary nor sufficient for persistence; what survivors share is less a state than a response, a slowing of whatever processes a given drug corrupts, beginning at the moment of exposure. This is not to exorcise dormancy from the story: in populations that have stopped growing for lack of nutrients, dormant cells do make up most of the survivors, and such populations are common in the chronic infections where persisters matter most. But the revision does jeopardize the hope of a single awakening treatment, since a cell that slows in response to the drug cannot be roused in advance of it.

Since the city added bicycle lanes along Harbor Avenue two years ago, the share of the avenue's reported traffic accidents that involve cyclists has risen from 8 percent to 14 percent. A council member concludes that the lanes have made Harbor Avenue more dangerous for the cyclists who use it.

Each of the forty musicians in the Halden Chamber Orchestra has won at least one international competition as a soloist. The Halden Chamber Orchestra must therefore be one of the finest orchestras performing today.

questions.prompt: Party leaders who had chosen the new governor because they expected her to be ___ learned within a month that she had an agenda of her own: she vetoed the first two bills they sent her and appointed none of their candidates.

explanation.key: The leaders picked her expecting what the vetoes then disproved: that she would be easy to manage. Tractable.

distractors.obstinate: Stubbornness is what she turned out to show, not what the leaders expected when they chose her.
distractors.venal: Expecting her to take bribes is not contradicted by vetoes and refused appointments specifically.
distractors.mercurial: Unpredictable moods would not be a reason to choose her.
distractors.erudite: Learning is not what an independent agenda contradicts.

questions.prompt: The committee's (i) ___ response to the first reports of contamination, a single paragraph promising to "monitor the situation", looked worse in hindsight than even a (ii) ___ one would have: had it acted before all the facts were in, it might have closed the wells before the leak reached three of them.

explanation.key: (i) A single paragraph promising only to watch is hasty and superficial: cursory. (ii) 'Even' and 'had it acted before all the facts were in' describe a response made without careful thought, which would still have beaten the actual one: rash.

distractors.exhaustive: A single paragraph is the opposite of thorough.
distractors.belligerent: Nothing about the response was hostile; it did too little.
distractors.measured: A careful response is what the committee claimed to be giving; 'even' calls for a worse kind of response that would still have been better.
distractors.tardy: The actual response was the late one; the contrast is with acting early.

questions.prompt: Visiting restorers mistook the villagers' refusal to clean the shrine's carvings for indifference, when it was the opposite: a scruple so (i) ___ that no one would lay a hand on the stone. The prohibition had remained (ii) ___ for generations only because nothing had ever tested it, and it became (iii) ___ the moment lichen began to eat the carvings and the village had to choose between custom and the carvings' survival.

explanation.key: (i) The opposite of indifference, so strong that no one would touch the stone: reverent. (ii) A rule that survived 'only because nothing had ever tested it' was kept intact, unbroken: inviolate. (iii) A forced choice between custom and survival turns an unquestioned rule into a disputed one: contentious.

distractors.perfunctory: Going through the motions is close to the indifference the restorers wrongly saw.
distractors.irreverent: Wrong polarity: the villagers' scruple is the opposite of indifference.
distractors.obsolete: An obsolete rule would not still be keeping hands off the stone.
distractors.provisional: Temporary; the rule had held for generations.
distractors.unanimous: A forced choice between custom and survival divides the village rather than uniting it.
distractors.dormant: The rule was active all along; the lichen made it disputed, not newly active.

questions.prompt: Collectors who boast that they have never been ___ by a forger are usually the least reliable judges of authenticity, since their confidence rests largely on the forgeries they failed to notice.

explanation.key: The forgeries they failed to notice fooled them without their knowing, so their boast is that they have never been deceived. Duped = hoodwinked.

distractors.cowed: Trap pair with intimidated: true synonyms that suit a boast, but fear has nothing to do with forgeries they failed to notice.
distractors.eclipsed: Being outshone is not what unnoticed forgeries show.
distractors.disparaged: A forger's belittling is unrelated to the logic.

questions.prompt: That both parties to the dispute cited the minister's statement the next morning as an endorsement of their own position testified less to her sympathy for either side than to how ___ her drafters had made it.

explanation.key: Each side read it as support, and the reason given is not sympathy, so the wording must allow more than one reading: ambiguous = equivocal.

distractors.conciliatory: Trap pair with placatory: they fit a minister's statement, but “less to her sympathy for either side” rules out a soothing gesture as the explanation.
distractors.lucid: A clear statement could not serve both sides.
distractors.strident: Wrong tone, and it would not explain the double reading.

questions.prompt: Visitors who knew the abbess only as a patron of devotional art were surprised less by the altarpieces in her private rooms than by the tavern scenes hanging beside them, for her taste proved ___ in a way that her commissions had never revealed.

explanation.key: Tavern scenes beside altarpieces show a range of taste wider than her devotional commissions suggested. Catholic in its secondary sense (wide-ranging) = eclectic.

distractors.pious: Trap pair with devout: they suit an abbess and devotional art, but piety is what visitors already knew; the surprise is the tavern scenes. The religious association also lures readers to misread “catholic”.
distractors.parochial: Narrow is the opposite of what the tavern scenes reveal.
distractors.recondite: Tavern scenes are not obscure or abstruse.

questions.prompt: In a firm where every other budget line had been cut twice, the research allowance remained ___, less because anyone defended it than because no manager wanted to be the first to propose touching it.

explanation.key: Every other line was cut, and nobody dared propose touching this one, so it was treated as untouchable: inviolate = sacrosanct.

distractors.trifling: Trap pair with negligible: an allowance can be small, but size does not explain why nobody dared to touch it.
distractors.robust: Near decoy: an uncut allowance may be healthy, but the clause is about its being untouchable, and robust has no partner.
distractors.extraneous: Irrelevance does not explain why it was spared.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the organization of the passage?
choices: A puzzle is posed, two competing accounts of it are presented, and evidence is cited that decides between them.

A phenomenon and its standard account are described along with a puzzle that account raises; an assumption of the account is then questioned, and an alternative is proposed and said to be compatible with it.
A phenomenon and its standard account are described along with a puzzle that account raises; an assumption of the account is then questioned, and an alternative is proposed and shown to supersede it.
An alternative account of a phenomenon is defended, and the standard account is then introduced as a rival that the evidence fails to support.
A standard account is presented, an objection to it is raised, and the objection is shown to rest on a misunderstanding of the phenomenon.

explanation.key: Paragraph 1: the phenomenon, the census account and the cheater puzzle. Paragraph 2: the census assumption is questioned (“often it does not”), the diffusion view is proposed, and then “the two readings need not be rivals”.

distractors.A puzzle is posed, two competing account: Nothing decides between the readings; the author says they need not be rivals.
distractors.A phenomenon and its standard account ar: One move off: the alternative is reconciled with the standard account, not shown to replace it.
distractors.An alternative account of a phenomenon i: Wrong order: the standard account comes first, and it is not rejected.
distractors.A standard account is presented, an obje: The objection (the signal need not track numbers) is upheld, not dismissed.

questions.prompt: Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply. The passage suggests which of the following about a mutant that benefits from the enzyme without producing it?
choices: Its advantage over cells that produce the enzyme would be smaller in a confined pore than the census reading by itself would lead one to expect.
It would eventually be eliminated from populations that live in confined spaces.
It would gain a further advantage by producing less of the signaling molecule as well.

explanation.key: A: yes. The census reading raises the cheater puzzle, but under confinement (close propinquity) a producer's enzyme returns mostly to itself and its kin, so the cheater gains less than the census reading implies. This takes two sentences of paragraph 2 together. B: no, one notch too strong; the problem is only “less acute”. C: no. Cheaters that also skimp on the signal exist in nature, but the passage never discusses signal production costs; true in the world, unsupported here.

questions.prompt: As the passage presents it, Galton's term “mediocrity” refers to

explanation.key: Both tall and short lineages move toward it, and it is the “type of its ancestors”, so it is the middle or average value, not poor quality.

distractors.inferior quality: The everyday sense; tall parents' children are not moving toward inferiority, and short parents' children move up toward the same point.
distractors.a lack of ambition: A personal trait, not a value that heights approach.
distractors.moderation in conduct: A moral sense, not a statistical one.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that reports a feature of Galton's own measurements that his hereditary explanation could not account for.

explanation.key: The fourth sentence (“Nor could Galton's force account for a fact his own tables contained…”) says outright that his tables show the pattern running backward, which a force acting on descendants cannot explain. The third sentence says only that the force is unnecessary, and it concerns correlated measurements in general, not Galton's own data.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an assumption on which the council member's argument relies?
choices: Most cyclists who travel on Harbor Avenue now ride in the new bicycle lanes.
The number of people cycling on Harbor Avenue has not risen enough since the lanes were added to account for the larger share of accidents involving cyclists.
Accidents involving cyclists on Harbor Avenue tend to be more serious than other accidents there.
Streets in the city that have no bicycle lanes have seen no change in the share of accidents involving cyclists.
Before the lanes were added, very few cyclists used Harbor Avenue at all.

explanation.key: 'More dangerous for the cyclists who use it' is a claim about each cyclist's risk. If many more people now cycle on the avenue, cyclists could make up more of the accidents while each one is safer. The argument needs the rise not to be explained by more cyclists; negated, B breaks it.

distractors.Most cyclists who travel on Harbor Avenu: The argument does not depend on where on the avenue the cyclists ride.
distractors.Accidents involving cyclists on Harbor A: Severity is not part of the reasoning about shares.
distractors.Streets in the city that have no bicycle: A comparison with other streets might strengthen the argument, but it is not required.
distractors.Before the lanes were added, very few cy: This would undercut the argument (more cyclists now), not support it.

questions.prompt: Biographers who call the publisher ___ rely on his letters to authors, in which he haggled over every advance; his account books tell a different story, recording anonymous gifts to the same authors in their leanest years.

explanation.key: Haggling over every advance is what the biographers rely on, so their label means stingy; the account books' secret gifts are what contradict it: parsimonious.

distractors.munificent: Generous is what the account books show, not what the letters suggest.
distractors.mercurial: Changeable moods are not what haggling shows.
distractors.punctilious: Attention to correct form does not follow from haggling and is not contradicted by gifts.
distractors.venal: Open to bribes; haggling over advances is not corruption.

questions.prompt: Had his hosts been less (i) ___ of his comfort, the ambassador might never have taken (ii) ___; but in his own country such care was lavished only on invalids, and he read their attentions as a verdict on his health.

explanation.key: “Such care” and “their attentions” show the hosts were eager about his comfort: solicitous. He read that care as a slight on his health, so he took offense: umbrage. The counterfactual says less care would have meant no offense.

distractors.heedless: The hosts lavished care, so they were not heedless; and “less heedless” would mean more care, the opposite of the counterfactual.
distractors.ill: A topic trap (invalids, health): his hosts' care did not make him ill; he read it as a judgment.
distractors.heart: Taking heart is the opposite of reading their care as an insult.

questions.prompt: The minister's (i) ___ public statements about the dam, praising its promise of cheap power in one speech and fretting over the displaced villages in the next, reflected genuine uncertainty rather than calculation. Her advisers, (ii) ___ of committing her before the engineers' report arrived, urged silence. When the report finally appeared, it bore out neither side wholesale: it (iii) ___ some of each side's claims and refuted others.

explanation.key: (i) Praise one day and worry the next, from 'genuine uncertainty': mixed feelings, ambivalent. (ii) Advisers who urge silence until the report arrives are cautious about committing her: wary. (iii) The report confirmed some claims and refuted others: it corroborated some.

distractors.unequivocal: Statements that swing between praise and worry are anything but clear-cut.
distractors.sanguine: Cheerfully optimistic; she fretted over the villages.
distractors.oblivious: Advisers who time her silence to the report are not unaware.
distractors.contemptuous: Scorn for committing her makes no sense with 'urged silence'.
distractors.fabricated: An engineers' report that invented claims would not 'bear out' anything.
distractors.suppressed: Suppressing claims is not the opposite of refuting them; the contrast needs confirming.

questions.prompt: After years of (i) ___ research, squeezed into odd months between teaching terms, the historian produced an (ii) ___ study, one that left later scholars little to add. Yet its conclusions were strikingly (iii) ___, as if the author, having read everything, trusted no single source enough to commit to it.

explanation.key: (i) Research done in odd months between terms was intermittent and unplanned: desultory. (ii) A study that left 'little to add' covered everything: exhaustive. (iii) 'Yet' and an author who 'trusted no single source enough to commit' point to hedged, uncommitted conclusions: tentative.

distractors.unflagging: Tireless and continuous; contradicted by 'odd months between teaching terms'.
distractors.clandestine: Secret research is not what the odd months describe.
distractors.cursory: A hasty study would leave much to add.
distractors.polemical: An argumentative study clashes with conclusions too cautious to commit.
distractors.dogmatic: Asserting opinions as certain is the opposite of refusing to commit.
distractors.derivative: Unoriginal does not fit a study that left later scholars little to add.

questions.prompt: Fifty years after the trial, a laboratory test of the preserved samples did what no appeal had managed: it ___ the dead chemist, showing that the poison could not have come from any compound his shop had ever stocked.

explanation.key: Showing the poison could not have come from his shop clears him of the crime that appeals had failed to overturn: vindicated and exonerated.

distractors.condemned: Trap pair with convicted: true synonyms for finding guilty, which the trial had already done; the test did the opposite.
distractors.convicted: Trap pair with condemned: wrong direction.
distractors.eulogized: Praising the dead is the bait of 'dead chemist'; a lab test clears, it does not praise.
distractors.exhumed: Digging up is the bait of 'preserved samples'; the samples were tested, not the chemist.

questions.prompt: The expedition's leader remained ___ even after the second supply drop failed, not because she discounted the danger, which she described to her team in unsparing detail, but because she had seen thinner margins survived.

explanation.key: “Even after” the failure she stayed hopeful, and the reason is experience, not denial: sanguine = buoyant (cheerfully optimistic in difficulty).

distractors.heedless: Trap pair with reckless: they suit a risky expedition, but “not because she discounted the danger” rules out disregard.
distractors.despondent: Wrong polarity: having seen thinner margins survived is a reason for hope.
distractors.taciturn: She described the danger in unsparing detail.

questions.prompt: Diplomats who prized the envoy did so not for his candor, which was considerable in private, but for public statements so ___ that each side could read them as the other's concession.

explanation.key: 'Not for his candor' sets the public statements against frankness, and statements each side reads as the other's concession are deliberately indirect and open to two readings: equivocal and oblique.

distractors.forthright: Trap pair with candid: true synonyms for frankness, the private quality the sentence sets aside.
distractors.candid: Trap pair with forthright: 'not for his candor'.
distractors.inflammatory: Statements both sides could read as gains would calm, not inflame.
distractors.verbose: Length is not what lets each side read a concession into them.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
choices: refute the revisionist claim that guild standards protected buyers who could not judge goods themselves
defend the economists' view of guilds as cartels against the objections of revisionist historians
argue that two opposing accounts of the guilds share an assumption that obscures conflict within the guilds
trace the rise of journeymen's brotherhoods as rivals to the guilds in the seventeenth century
reconcile the economists' and the revisionists' accounts by showing that each describes the guilds of a different period

explanation.key: “Both accounts, however, treat the guild as a single actor”: the court records show master–journeyman conflict, and the guild is “less an actor than an arena”.

distractors.refute the revisionist claim that guild: Wrong verb: “None of this shows that the revisionists are wrong about information or training.”
distractors.defend the economists' view of guilds as: The author faults the economists' view on the same ground as the revisionists'.
distractors.trace the rise of journeymen's brotherho: Too narrow: the brotherhoods are evidence inside paragraph 2.
distractors.reconcile the economists' and the revisi: No division by period; the author rejects the premise both share.

questions.prompt: The author's attitude toward the revisionist historians' account of the guilds is best described as
choices: acceptance of the evidence on which it rests, together with a belief that it goes too far in rejecting the economists' view
admiration for its correction of the economists, tempered by the belief that it holds only for trades whose goods buyers could not judge
acceptance of its claims about what guilds provided, combined with the view that it shares a misleading premise with the account it opposes
qualified approval of its method, coupled with doubt that its claims about apprenticeship are accurate
scathing rejection of its claim that guild standards protected buyers

explanation.key: The author grants the information and training claims (“None of this shows that the revisionists are wrong…”) but says that both accounts wrongly treat the guild as a single actor.

distractors.acceptance of the evidence on which it r: Half-right: the author never says the revisionists should have kept more of the cartel view; a rule “can protect buyers and exclude rivals at once” corrects both.
distractors.admiration for its correction of the eco: Invents a limit of scope; the author's reservation is about the single-actor premise.
distractors.qualified approval of its method, couple: Reverses the stance: the author accepts the training claim.
distractors.scathing rejection of its claim that gui: Far too strong, and the wrong polarity.

questions.prompt: Consider each of the choices separately and select all that apply. The passage indicates which of the following about the requirements for admission to mastership?
choices: They were not applied equally to all candidates.
They grew more costly to meet during the seventeenth century.
They were adopted chiefly in order to keep the number of masters small.

explanation.key: A: yes; masters' sons and sons-in-law “were routinely excused from them”. B: yes; the cost of the masterpiece, fee and banquet “rose through the seventeenth century”. C: no. The standards “also kept the number of masters small”, which is an effect, not a stated purpose, and the last sentence warns against reading statutes as the intention of one party.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is most closely analogous to the assumption that the author attributes to the Western collectors?
choices: A publisher markets a cookbook under a celebrity chef's name, although a staff of writers developed and tested its recipes.
A historian argues that a treaty named after one diplomat was in fact negotiated by his staff, so that his name on it is merely a convenience.
A listener credits a pianist with the warmth of a recording's sound, although that warmth was produced by the engineer's choice of microphones.
A collector pays more for early printings of a book because later printings introduced errors.
A critic refuses to judge a building until she knows which of the architect's assistants drew its plans.

explanation.key: The collectors' assumption is that the name on a work identifies the source of every quality a viewer admires in it. The listener credits the named performer with a quality that someone else in the production supplied.

distractors.A publisher markets a cookbook under a c: Matches the publishers' practice (putting a selling name on the work), not the viewers' inference about where admired qualities come from.
distractors.A historian argues that a treaty named a: Parallels the recent scholarship that calls the designer's preeminence a fiction, not the collectors.
distractors.A collector pays more for early printing: Shares only the surface feature of early versus late impressions.
distractors.A critic refuses to judge a building unt: The opposite habit: attention to collaborators.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that
choices: Western collectors were the first to treat the designer as the principal author of a print
the name of a popular designer had commercial value in Japan before Western collectors began buying the prints
later impressions of a print are generally inferior to earlier impressions of the same design
carvers and printers resented the prominence that publishers gave to designers
the recent scholarship the author mentions is mistaken in holding that carvers and printers shaped the qualities of a print

explanation.key: Publishers advertised series under designers “popular enough to sell them”, and the cult of the designer “was not simply imported”, so the name was already selling prints in Japan before the collectors of the 1860s arrived. This takes two sentences together.

distractors.Western collectors were the first to tre: Contradicted: the publishers had already done so.
distractors.later impressions of a print are general: One example of a lost gradation, stated as a general rule; true of many prints in the world, unsupported here.
distractors.the recent scholarship the author mentio: The author agrees they did; the reservation is about calling the designer's preeminence a foreign fiction.

questions.prompt: Select the sentence that limits the scope of a conclusion the author has just drawn.

explanation.key: The seventh sentence (“This is not to exorcise dormancy from the story…”) follows the conclusion that dormancy is neither necessary nor sufficient, and keeps dormancy as the main route to survival in starved populations. The second sentence qualifies what persisters are, but no conclusion has yet been drawn; the last sentence draws a further consequence instead of limiting one.

questions.prompt: The passage states each of the following about persisters EXCEPT:
choices: Their offspring are no more resistant to the drug than the population from which they came.
Some of them were dividing shortly before they were exposed to the drug.
They survive by slowing processes that the drug disrupts.
They are more numerous in chronic infections than in acute ones.
They are not, as a rule, genetic mutants resistant to the drug.

explanation.key: The passage says starved populations are common in chronic infections and that persisters “matter most” there; it never compares their numbers in chronic and acute infections.

distractors.Their offspring are no more resistant to: Stated: regrowth is “as susceptible as the original”; “their offspring inherit no protection”.
distractors.Some of them were dividing shortly befor: Stated: “many persisters had been dividing just before the drug arrived”.
distractors.They survive by slowing processes that t: Stated: “a slowing of whatever processes a given drug corrupts”.

questions.prompt: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: assumes that what is true of each member of a group must be true of the group as a whole
relies on the judgment of critics who may be biased in the orchestra's favor
takes for granted that soloists are more accomplished than other musicians
fails to consider that the orchestra may have recently replaced some of its musicians
confuses the size of an orchestra with the quality of its playing

explanation.key: That every player is a fine soloist does not show that they play well together; ensemble playing needs things (blend, discipline, a shared conception) that no individual's skill guarantees. The argument moves from the parts to the whole.

distractors.relies on the judgment of critics who ma: No critics are cited; the premise is about the players' own accomplishments.
distractors.takes for granted that soloists are more: The argument needs no ranking of soloists against other players.
distractors.fails to consider that the orchestra may: The premise is about the current musicians, so turnover does not matter.
